subject: english-literature
title: Critical Vocabulary Stretch
welcome_lead: Push into top-band vocabulary: didactic, polemical, satirical, and the difference an examiner notices.
meta_desc: GCSE English Literature — stretch critical vocabulary: didactic, polemical, satirical, allegorical.
final_note: You can now choose precise tonal labels and avoid the vague 'the writer makes us feel.'.

concepts.def: Intended to teach a moral or political lesson
Strongly arguing against an opposing view
Using humour to attack folly or vice
Carrying a deeper symbolic moral meaning
Belonging to a threshold or in-between state

walkthroughs.body_html:
A didactic text teaches; a polemical text attacks.

A Christmas Carol is both: it teaches charity (didactic) and attacks Malthusian indifference (polemical). Using both terms shows you can see two layers.

Satire uses humour to attack.

Priestley's Birling sounds pompous when he says 'a man has to mind his own business' — a satirical portrait of the smug capitalist. Naming the technique sharpens your point.

Liminal means 'on the threshold.'

Scrooge's bedchamber visits, the witches' heath, the Inspector's doorway — all liminal spaces where the rules shift. Spotting them lets you write about transformation precisely.

options: Designed to teach a moral lesson

mcqs.q: Which word best describes a text using humour to attack folly?

numericals.q: How many of the six concepts above describe a TONE or PURPOSE of a writer?
numericals.hint: Didactic, polemical and satirical all describe purpose.

free_texts.q: What single word means 'belonging to a threshold or in-between state'?
